### Problem: minimum depth of a binary tree {#sec-tr-p1-min}

::: {.p-statement}
Return the number of nodes on the shortest root-to-leaf path. A leaf has no children. A node with one child is not a leaf.

Constraints: up to $10^5$ nodes.

Source: [LC 111 · Minimum Depth of Binary Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-depth-of-binary-tree/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
`1 + min` of both sides treats a missing child as a leaf of depth $0$, so a right spine of five nodes reports $1$. Recurse into a side only when that child exists. Level order can stop at the first leaf and never visit the rest of a wide tree.
:::

::: {#fig-tr-min}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):

    root = V.Node("3", [
        V.Node("9", color="green"),
        V.Node("20", [V.Node("15"), V.Node("7")], color="amber"),
    ], color="green")
    V.tree(ax, p, root, dx=1.15, dy=1.3, size=10)

V.show(draw)
```

The sample. The shortest root-to-leaf path is $3, 9$, two nodes. Treating the missing right child of $9$ as a leaf of depth $0$ is what a bare `1 + min` does; this tree's right side is simply longer, and the answer is still $2$.

:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Recursion.** Null returns $0$. One missing child: return `1 +` the other side. Both present: return `1 +` the smaller of the two.
2. **First leaf.** BFS by levels. The level of the first node with no children is the answer, and deeper nodes stay in the queue unvisited only if you return immediately.

**Invariant.** The number returned for $u$ is the node-count of a shortest downward path from $u$ to a leaf. A missing child contributes no path.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

The measuring template, with the minimum taken only over children that exist.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def min_depth(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    if root.left is None:
        return 1 + min_depth(root.right)
    if root.right is None:
        return 1 + min_depth(root.left)
    return 1 + min(min_depth(root.left), min_depth(root.right))
```

##### C++

```cpp
int minDepth(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    if (!root->left) return 1 + minDepth(root->right);
    if (!root->right) return 1 + minDepth(root->left);
    return 1 + std::min(minDepth(root->left), minDepth(root->right));
}
```

:::

#### First leaf

::: {.form-next}
Same answer, computed downward. Stop at the first leaf the level order meets. A path of $10^5$ nodes is a comfortable loop and an uncomfortable recursion.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get('min', 'bfs')
    assert str(final) == '2'
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def min_depth_bfs(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0
    q = deque([(root, 1)])
    while q:
        u, d = q.popleft()
        if u.left is None and u.right is None:
            return d
        if u.left:
            q.append((u.left, d + 1))
        if u.right:
            q.append((u.right, d + 1))
    return 0


spine = from_level([2, None, 3, None, 4, None, 5, None, 6])
assert min_depth(spine) == 5 and min_depth_bfs(spine) == 5
assert min_depth(None) == 0 and min_depth(Node(1)) == 1
assert min_depth(from_level([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == 2
for n in range(1, 40):
    root = complete_tree(n)
    assert min_depth(root) == min_depth_bfs(root)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int minDepthBfs(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return 0;
    queue<pair<TreeNode*, int>> q;
    q.push({root, 1});
    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto [u, d] = q.front();
        q.pop();
        if (!u->left && !u->right) return d;
        if (u->left) q.push({u->left, d + 1});
        if (u->right) q.push({u->right, d + 1});
    }
    return 0;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
Both forms are $O(n)$ time in the worst case. The BFS examines only the nodes down to the first leaf, so a shallow leaf on the left of a huge tree returns early. Extra memory is $O(h)$ for the recursion and $O(\text{width})$ for the queue.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A right spine `[2,null,3,null,4,null,5,null,6]` has minimum depth $5$. The naive `1 + min` of both sides, with null as $0$, returns $1$.
- One node is a leaf of depth $1$. The empty tree is $0$.
- `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` has a leaf at depth $2$ (the node $9$) and deeper leaves on the right. The answer is $2$, not the maximum $3$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- `1 + min` of both sides treats a missing child as depth $0$, so `[1, 2]` and a right spine both report $1$.
- An answer off by one is nodes versus edges. This problem counts nodes: one node is $1$, and the empty tree is $0$.
- Calling the recursion twice, once to compare and once to return, recomputes the subtree. Keep the two depths.
:::

**Variants.** The sum of the values on the deepest level keeps a pair (depth, sum) and adds the sums only on a tie: [LC 1302 · Deepest Leaves Sum](https://leetcode.com/problems/deepest-leaves-sum/){difficulty="Medium"}. The leftmost value on the last level is the first node of the last BFS round: [LC 513 · Find Bottom Left Tree Value](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-bottom-left-tree-value/){difficulty="Medium"}. The same height read off a parent array is the forward pass in @sec-tr-p4.
